newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italy local vote brings relief all round.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italy local vote brings relief all round.

text.p: The opposition took control of Milan, Italy's second city, in local elections but wins for the governing centre-left elsewhere pointed to an honourable draw ahead of key decisions on Europe and the economy.
Results on Monday from Sunday's second-round mayoral run-offs in 77 cities and towns brought smiles all round from the national political blocs, allowing everybody to cry victory.

The vote was the first significant test of sentiment since Prime Minister Romano Prodi's appointment one year ago and of the public mood after 12 months of tough budgetary action to try to squeeze Italy into the start of Europe's single currency.
Milan, Italy's financial capital and previously held by the separatist Northern League, was the jewel in the crown in the contests, which included 10 big cities.
It went to the centre-right Freedom Alliance. Its candidate, industrialist Gabriele Albertini, defeated centre-left Olive Tree rival Aldo Fumagalli with 53.1 percent of the vote.
In Turin, Olive Tree incumbent Valentino Castellani was narrowly re-elected with 50.4 percent of votes after striking an electoral pact with the hard-left party Communist Refoundation.
Prodi relies on Refoundation for a parliamentary majority but ideological differences, especially on public spending and pensions, have made for a rocky relationship.
The Freedom Alliance and political commentators said the Turin result showed the Olive Tree could not succeed without the hard left.

They argued that the result in Turin, Italy's industrial capital and home of car giant Fiat, could strengthen Refoundation's hand in a looming showdown over reductions to welfare spending the government is contemplating to cut the budget deficit sufficiently to join Europe's monetary union.

"It is obvious that the forces...which support the government will have to assess now who counts for more and who for less," said Gianfranco Fini, leader of the Freedom Alliance's hard-right member party, the National Alliance.
"All commentators agree that the results in Milan and Turin show that the Olive Tree only wins if it allies with Communist Refoundation," he said.
The Olive Tree rejected the claim, saying the local tests would have no impact on the balance of forces.
The Olive Tree's Fumagalli refused to do a deal with Refoundation in Milan, and lost, but in three other cities where no electoral pact was struck, the centre-left won.
They included the northeast port of Trieste, where incumbent mayor and coffee magnate Riccardo Illy held on with 53.9 percent of the vote.

In all, the Olive Tree won four of the 10 big contests and the Freedom Alliance four, The Northern League, whose incumbent mayor in Milan was trounced in the first round on April 27, won in the northern towns of Lecco and Pordenone.
Deputy Prime Minister Walter Veltroni said the outcome was a vindication for the government's austerity drive to prepare Italy for the planned single currency.
"For us...it is a confirmation of the consent of public opinion to the action we are undertaking," Veltroni said.
Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti said the voting showed his party was indispensable to the centre-left.

The centre-left coalition is due to start talks with union leaders on Tuesday over possible changes to social spending and many economists are urging a fresh overhaul of pensions, just two years after the last reform of the generous state system.

"The future of the Prodi government depends on the welfare state. We hope that the ruling majority consolidates itself around the question of social reform," Bertinotti said, repeating that welfare spending should not be cut.
